status_summary: The 2026 National Defense Strategy (posted 2026-01-23 on media.defense.gov) orders four lines of effort: defend the homeland first, deter China in the Indo-Pacific second, increase burden-sharing with allies third, and strengthen the defense industrial base fourth. Compared with the Mandate (pp. 92-94), the commitment to deny aggression along the First Island Chain and the push for allies in Europe and Korea to lead their own conventional defense with a smaller supporting U.S. role match in substance. The ranking differs, because the Mandate puts China first and the strategy puts the homeland first, and the strategy does not mention Taiwan, which the Mandate names as the focus of the denial defense and of force planning. NATO allies agreed at The Hague on 2025-06-25 to reach 5 percent of GDP in defense and related spending by 2035. On posture, the FY2026 NDAA (Public Law 119-60, 2025-12-18) has sections on oversight of U.S. posture in Europe and on the Korean Peninsula and bars, per an Atlantic Council guide, funds to cut forces in Europe below 76,000 or in South Korea below 28,500 without certification or reporting, which limits the smaller Europe posture the Mandate recommends. The Defense Department said in May 2026 that it would permanently cut about 4,000 soldiers in Europe, and on 2026-07-28 it launched a posture review of up to six months aimed at moving NATO toward primary responsibility for its conventional defense.

timeline.event: A classified interim defense guidance (March 2025; day not given, first of month used) reportedly named a Taiwan denial scenario as the pacing scenario, per CSIS's January 2026 analysis.
timeline.source: Center for Strategic and International Studies

timeline.event: NATO leaders at The Hague commit to 5 percent of GDP annually by 2035: at least 3.5 percent for core defense and up to 1.5 percent for related security spending, with a review in 2029. (Summit held 2025-06-24 to 2025-06-25; the declaration page fetched does not show a date.)

The FY2026 NDAA becomes Public Law 119-60 (date shown on govinfo.gov); its table of contents lists Sec. 1249 (oversight of United States military posture in Europe) and Sec. 1268 (oversight of United States military posture on the Korean Peninsula). An Atlantic Council guide dated 2025-12-17, the day the Senate passed the bill, describes the provisions as barring funds to cut U.S. forces in Europe below 76,000 or in South Korea below 28,500 without certification or reporting.

The Department releases the 2026 National Defense Strategy. It ranks homeland defense first and deterring China second among four lines of effort, commits to denying aggression along the First Island Chain, does not mention Taiwan, and gives Europe and South Korea the lead on their own conventional defense with a smaller supporting U.S. role.

The Defense Department says it will permanently cut about 4,000 soldiers from Europe, reducing Army brigade combat teams there from four to three; a spokesman says the aim is to get NATO allies to lead Europe's conventional defense.

Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby announces a force posture review of up to six months aimed at moving NATO toward European allies leading their own conventional defense; Stripes reports the Army ended a rotational brigade mission in Romania in October 2025 and cancelled an armored brigade deployment to Poland in May 2026.

A statement of Under Secretary Elbridge Colby on implementation of the 2026 National Defense Strategy is submitted to the Senate Armed Services Committee (document posted on media.defense.gov; not opened here, so its content was not used).

title: Make China the top defense priority and shift conventional defense burdens to allies
uncertainties: The 2026 National Defense Strategy was read through a browser retrieval supplied to the project; direct fetches by the research tools and by the independent reviewer failed (no HTTP 429), so the strategy content rests on that retrieval, which also reports no occurrence of Taiwan in the text. The publication date comes from the hosting address, not from the document text. Element-by-element comparison with Mandate pp. 92-94: matches are the denial posture along the First Island Chain and allied primary responsibility for conventional defense in Europe and Korea with U.S. support more limited; partial matches are the burden-sharing line of effort (the Mandate calls it central, the strategy ranks it third) and the nuclear and counterterrorism items, which were not compared in detail; differences are the top priority (homeland in the strategy, China in the Mandate) and the absence of Taiwan and of a force-planning construct built on a Taiwan scenario. The strategy also does not use the phrase irregular warfare. The March 2025 classified guidance is known only through CSIS. The NDAA was checked only through section titles; the 76,000 and 28,500 floors come from the Atlantic Council guide and the section text was not read. The 2026-09-28 statement to the Senate Armed Services Committee was not opened. The Bloomberg Government text was paywalled after the first paragraphs, and Stripes separately cites a cut of 5,000 troops from Germany, a figure not reconciled or used. The two sources differ on the Europe floor exception (certification versus a 45-day limit). I did not verify whether the NDAA certification was used for the May 2026 cut, or any posture changes in Korea, Japan or the Gulf. Whether the strategy moves toward the Mandate is a judgment: it matches on denial defense and burden-sharing but not on China as the first priority or on Taiwan.
